content.text:
Karen Massey
COO, argenx SE
How the business mix will evolve between IV and subcutaneous. We will be focusing on keeping them both on the market and providing that choice to patients and prescribers.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Yatin Suneja from Guggenheim. Your line is open.
Yatin Suneja
Senior Biotechnology Analyst, Guggenheim
Hi, thank you for taking my question. Question on the CIDP study. Are you willing to share the relative mix of the, basically, the baseline of the CIDP patient, how that might look relative to the first 40-patient baseline that you had shared? If you can't answer it, I wanted to ask about Europe, especially as it relates to the gMG launch. Like, what are some of the major hurdles for you to really accelerate the uptake in Europe similar to what you're seeing in the US? Thank you so much.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Thank you, Yatin, for your two questions. On the first one, the answer is simple. I think we'll need to wait for the top-line data released because we don't have that information at this point in time. Rest assured that in the typical style of the house, we will release top-line data such that there will be sufficient clarity about the context and the meaning of the data. With regards to hurdles to a European launch, maybe, Karl, this is a question which you feel comfortable to take.
Karl Gubitz
CFO, argenx SE
Yeah. Thank you, Tim. I would say that the main hurdles, of course, is the pricing and reimbursement processes. We have only launched in Germany and that is through the AMNOG process, where we are still negotiating the price throughout the 12 months. That leads to some physicians in Germany have a natural conservatism as we go through this process. But that said, if we look at Germany, the unmet need is definitely there. The feedback we get back from physicians and patients are really positive. In terms of the rest of Europe, we say that we are in pricing and reimbursement discussions in more than 10 countries, but basically all the European countries. We are in various stages of it.
We hope to conclude some of those processes before the end of the year, but really from a planning perspective, we see it more as 2024 launches. That is basically the main hurdle. I just wanna end back with the unmet need is there, and the initial feedback from the payers, the physicians, and the patients where we have it is really positive, and we look forward to successful launches, but it will take time to get there.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Akash Tewari from Jefferies. Your line is open.
Akash Tewari
Global Head of Biopharmaceutical Research, Jefferies
Hey, thanks so much. So just, number one, any color on exactly when you hit the 88 events for CIDP? And on the placebo arm, you know, what signals are you seeing internally that gives you confidence that placebo's behaving kind of like the PATH study did and not a kind of bearish scenario where relapse rates are trending more in the 40% to 50% range? Thank you.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Hey, thank you, Akash. Thanks for being with us today. We're not giving any more granularity on exactly when these 88 events happened. I also don't think that's important. I think the most important fact is that we now have them, and from now actually we're in control of the final steps in the process. We're not aware of any data, so we will need to wait for placebo data until we see the data, and we're then ready, of course, to present them to all of you. Stay tuned. We will be talking about placebo during the top-line release. Thank you.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Thomas Smith from SVB Securities. Your line is open.
Thomas Smith
Senior Research Analyst, SVB Securities
Hey, guys. Good morning. Thanks for taking the questions. You mentioned work going on in the background on a next gen subcutaneous presentation of efgartigimod. I was just wondering if you could provide a little bit more details. Is this still using the enhanced enabled technology? Maybe if you could provide an update on the Elektrofi collaboration, that would be super helpful. Thanks.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Yeah, Thomas, thank you for the question. I think we've published on the fact that we're gonna launch with a kind of first-generation subQ, which is a pull-up product from the vial, like so many other product executions look. We are of course diligently working on a pre-filled syringe. That is the next generation, you're alluding to. You know that this company likes to plan for the long haul, so we're working on multiple product presentations, including of course subQ product presentations. That's where you have to contextualize the Elektrofi collaboration. More on that, you know, when we're more advanced in the process. Multiple generations in the works, not just for Vyvgart, but also be applicable to other pipeline assets. Thank you.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Danielle Brill from Raymond James. Your line is open.
Danielle Brill
Biotechnology Sector Analyst, Raymond James
Hi, guys. Good morning. Thank you for the question. It sounds like you're launching the subQ before we have top-line CIDP data. I'm just curious how this impacts your thinking on pricing strategy for the subQ?
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Hey, Danielle. Thanks for being with us today, and thank you for the pricing question. Typically, we don't give any color on pricing, you know, until the date of launch. I would encourage you to have a few months patience to see, you know, how we're launching and the commitment of the company is, of course, to give you transparency on positioning of the product, and pricing at the day of launch. Okay? Bear with us.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Joel Beatty from Baird. Your line is open.
Joel Beatty
Biotechnology Equity Research Analyst, Baird
Great, thanks. For the CIDP trial, what's most important to achieve for the trial to be considered a success?
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Hey, Joel, thanks for being with us. The way we have been calibrating expectations is by taking our audience back to the historical IVIG registration trials. What we have been talking about is, you know, the type of data coming out of the ADHERE study, which would put us in a position to effectively compete with IVIG. We would be triangulating towards kind of 50% response in stage A, and I think an effect size of 20% to 30% difference between active and placebo in stage B. I think that would put us in a position to effectively compete with IVIG. That's a comparable efficacy, roughly speaking. You know, of course, that, you know, the product will also be judged by its risks. It's not just the benefit, also the risks.
I think we're offering a very safe and tolerable product. Of course, convenience, which will be a game changer, comparing, you know, a 32, 120 seconds dose injection compared to a life which is basically organized around the infusion chair. I hope this answers your question.
Joel Beatty
Biotechnology Equity Research Analyst, Baird
Thank you.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Alex Thompson from Stifel. Your line is open.
Alex Thompson
Managing Director, Stifel
Hey, great. Thanks for taking my question. I was hoping maybe you could provide a little bit more details around sort of the current patient mix in the US on Vyvgart. Can you talk a little bit about the proportion of patients that are, you know, on drug that are IVIG naive? And then maybe if you would comment on whether you're seeing any meaningful off-label use, either in sort of non-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive patients or in other indications. Thanks.
Karen Massey
COO, argenx SE
Yeah, this is Karen. I can provide some of those answers. What we've seen since launch is that we've been progressively moving it up to earlier line patients. More momentum after orals and ISTs. In terms of the IVIG, around 50% to 55% of our patients currently are coming from IVIG. As I mentioned earlier, our strategy is to continue to move earlier in the treatment paradigm. In terms of off-label, we don't track that data. We don't support off-label use of the product through PSP, but from what we understand, we don't see significant off-label use.
Alex Thompson
Managing Director, Stifel
Great. Thanks.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Allison Bratzel from Piper Sandler. Your line is open.
Allison Bratzel
Director and Senior Research Analyst, Piper Sandler
Hi, good morning, and thank you for taking my questions. Just a commercial question on Vyvgart. Could you comment on any, you know, Q1 seasonal effects you saw, with, you know, payer resets or reverification of benefits? Was that a meaningful factor in the quarter, at least in the US? Any color there would be helpful. Thanks.
Karen Massey
COO, argenx SE
Thanks for the question. As with other products, we did see recertifications in January. As you all well know, we have very strong payer access for Vyvgart. What we saw was some slowdown in January, but really those patients were back on therapy February or March. It was really more of a push by a month or two rather than anything more.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Yaron Werber from Cowen. Your line is open.
Yaron Werber
Managing Director and Biotechnology Research Analyst, Cowen
Great. I have a question on CIDP. It's sort of a two-part question that's interrelated. The first one, can you give us a little bit of a sense? I mean, that you only really stopped recruiting back in February. So it sounds to us like you probably ended up recruiting close to 180 patients, so the upper end of the study. Is that correct? And then secondly, when you're talking about just, you know, before you able to lock the database, and moving patients to the open-label extension, how does that work? It's not. It doesn't happen automatically at week 48, or you're referring to really now taking all the placebo patients and moving them over, whatever remaining patients there are.
I'm just trying to understand, you know, why that's gonna take a little bit longer than normal. Thank you.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Yeah. Thank you, Yaron. Thank you for the question. You correctly call out that we continue to enroll patients to the trial, even if we thought that we had sufficient patients in stage B to ultimately hit the 88 events. You will see the final details of the patients we effectively enrolled to, you know, the run-in stage A and stage B when we do the top-line data readout. The rollover mechanics are relatively complicated in that sense that a patient has an option to either go to the open-label extension or not go over to the open-label extension, and then you need to do some close out visits, you need to collect some final information, et cetera. You have the decision fork in the roads, and it just involves, you know, confirmatory visits, data collection.
Basically, the study is in the shape, and you can say, "Okay, we have all the data into lock the database and go with, you know, quality data to a top-line data readout." Okay? I hope that makes sense. Thank you, Yaron.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Samantha Semenkow from Citi. Your line is open.
Samantha Semenkow
SMid Biotech Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Thank you very much for taking our question. You're not talking about the 180 patients that you're enrolling in it here. You aren't gonna give any additional details on that at this time. Maybe could you just talk about, sorry, excuse me. I have to get off on here.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
This will be an opportunity for me to finish up on Yaron's question. Once there is an event happening, of course, as a patient, you can make the decision to roll over or basically exit the study, so you don't have to be 48 weeks in the study. It is an event-driven trial, not a time-driven trial. I hope that that answers also the question which we have from Citi. Let's move on. Thank you.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Myles Minter from William Blair. Your line is open.
Myles Minter
Biotechnology Research Analyst, William Blair
Thanks for taking the question. It's actually on the Genmab collaboration. Just curious as to how dedicated you are stepping into oncology in the joint venture. I know previously, you sort of out-licensed an asset to AbbVie, but just wondering whether that's a pillar outside of immunology or tangential to that argenx is really dedicated to, or is Genmab really the lead on that oncology asset and you're focusing on the immunology part of that deal? Thanks very much.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Hey, Myles. Thank you. Thanks for that question. That's a great question. The way you need to think about our Genmab collaboration is in the context of our IIP program. You know, we are externally focused. We like to partner with expert partners externally to go after novel target biology. This is just an interesting immunology pathway where we see utility in both autoimmunity and oncology. We think there's a real exciting increase in probability of success by joining forces. I mean, two antibody powerhouses with pretty complementary technology platforms and expertise. We're having a go at this pathway. We will basically go in there 50/50. We will share any investments and cost 50/50, and we will share any upside 50/50. Whenever there is upside in oncology, we can share. Whenever there's upside in autoimmunity, we can share.
That is the gist of the collaboration more than anything else. Okay? Thank you for your question.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Niall Alexander from Deutsche Bank. Your line is open.
Niall Alexander
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Hi, guys. It's Niall Alexander from Deutsche Bank. It'd be good to get your views on how sales trends will evolve and, as we get for the year, in the US and in the European regions. Thanks.
Karen Massey
COO, argenx SE
Yeah. This is Karen. I can comment on that. As Karl mentioned earlier, we won't be providing guidance, but in terms of the trends, we've seen consistent growth and momentum in the US market, and we expect that to continue as we move to early aligned patients, and through the year. Karl already shared some thoughts on the European market. We're pursuing pricing and reimbursement, and so we think that will be a slower growth trajectory. It's also very important to note that we do have competition coming later in the year, and so that will be a further unknown factor. We're confident in our efficacy, safety, and convenience profile that we can establish as those competitors come into the market.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Suzanne van Voorthuizen from Kempen & Company. Your line is open.
Suzanne van Voorthuizen
Head of Life Sciences Research, Kempen and Company
Hi, team. This is Suzanne. Thanks for taking my questions. I was wondering beyond efgartigimod for ARGX-117 in the upcoming mid-2023 data release. Can you give some more granularity? This is the first cohort readout. How many patients are in that? How many are on drug and placebo, the doses that you're testing and, you know, what other cohorts are there in this study next? I have a follow-up after that.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
That's great, Suzanne. It's an excellent question. Of course, ARGX-117 is a molecule we're very excited about. The way you have to think about the phase II trial is the following. Nobody has any idea what level of C2 inhibition one needs to have a clinical effect in MMN patients. What we really try to build is a PK/PD model based on the phase II data, which can reliably predict the phase III dose in MMN, assuming, of course, the molecule is gonna work in MMN. Think of Cohort 1, the data we will be talking about mid of the year as a first dose and dosing regimen cohort, where we're aiming for a certain percentage of C2 inhibition.
We will be talking about nine patients in total, where we will basically have an idea now for that type of C2 inhibition, what clinical efficacy you can expect. Based on those data, we have an option to either up the dose or lower the dose to then conclude the phase II trial. Remember, all MMN patients which we are realistically able to attract to the trial are basically on IVIG. This is, again, going to be kind of randomized, a trial design, where we basically see a stable cadence on IVIG for these patients, and then they get randomized after a running period, either on ARGX-117 or on placebo. We hope to see that we can keep these IVIG patients stable on ARGX-117.
While, of course, you would expect the placebo patients to need retreatment after a while with IVIG. That's the type of data we're going to talk about. You had another question.
Suzanne van Voorthuizen
Head of Life Sciences Research, Kempen and Company
Yes. Thanks a lot. That's very helpful. I just have one clarification question on the ADAPT+ data presentation at AAN. There seem to have been more adverse events of grade three or higher than before. Were those related to the COVID-19 infections or is there any other color you can give on this? Thanks.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
There is, of course, a caveat here, Suzanne. The open-label extension is much longer, of course, than the randomized controlled trial. The absolute number of events is going up because you're just measuring over longer periods of time. I invite you to look at the column that we normalize per time unit. You will actually see that the safety profile of Vyvgart continues to be very clean and in line with the ADAPT study itself. I think the news of this post is outstanding. We have now multiple years of experience with Vyvgart, by the way, not just in myasthenia gravis, but across many indications, and the safety profile is consistent and encouraging. I think this is setting a whole new standard in terms of benefit risk profile in the severe autoimmune space. Thank you.
Suzanne van Voorthuizen
Head of Life Sciences Research, Kempen and Company
Got it. Thanks.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Trevor Allred from Oppenheimer. Your line is open.
Trevor Allred
Executive Director and Analyst, Oppenheimer
Hey, thanks for taking the question. Just wanted to ask, so Tepezza had a miss earlier, just a few days ago. Wanted to see if you had any updated thoughts on the opportunity there and where efgartigimod fits in. Thanks.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Trevor, we don't feel we're sufficiently informed to talk about sales dynamics behind Tepezza. I think this would be a question best asked to Horizon. We repeat, you know, our conviction in the indication and the reason we selected that indication for Vyvgart is based on solid biology understanding, and then of course, the feasibility of running clinical trials and the remaining unmet medical needs. Thank you for the question.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Douglas Tsao from HCW. Your line is open.
Douglas Tsao
Managing Director of Equity Research, HCW
Hi. Good morning. Thanks for taking questions and congrats on the progress, Tim. So maybe just for ARGX-117 as well as ARGX-119, I'm just curious because you've identified or sort of named a you know, three indications for ARGX-117. You sort of noted a couple potential ones for 119. How quickly after those initial studies do you think you might ramp into other indications? I say that just because with efgartigimod, we very quickly went from MG to a full pipeline of over you know, double-digit number of ongoing trials. Do you see the same potential for those assets? And do we think that you know, efgartigimod represents a roadmap for how quickly we might see the development programs for those assets expand? Thank you.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Thank you, Doug. I appreciate the question. You're right. When we select pipeline assets, we love to go from novel biology. We like to do that with what we think will ultimately be best-in-class antibody molecules. We like optionality, so we love molecules which can play in multiple indications. What ultimately the number of indications is gonna be for ARGX-117 and ARGX-119, we do not know yet. We think there is sufficient opportunity in front of us. You know that we like to march based on conviction on the biology. Rest assured that argenx is doing its homework from a biology point of view on opportunity above and beyond the indications we mentioned. We will inform you when we see sufficient ground to expand beyond the initial indications. Thanks for the question.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Joon Lee from Truist Securities. Your line is open.
Joon Lee
Managing Director and Biotech Analyst, Truist Securities
Hey, congrats on the quarter, and thanks for taking our question. For the planned TED trial, it's sort of interesting to consider the possibility that targeting FcRn could address not just the ocular manifestations, but also, you know, the systemic manifestations of hyperthyroidism. Along that line, would you consider an endpoint other than proptosis for possibly a broader label? As a follow-up, is there any data out there pointing to how much IgG reduction you would need to have a clinical impact on proptosis? Thank you.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Yeah. Thank you, Joon, for the question. I'd love to answer it, but the commitment we made during the JPMorgan conference was that clinical trial design details will be disclosed when the study will go online on ClinicalTrials.gov. I encourage us to be a little bit patient, and then we can talk about primary, secondary endpoints, inclusion, exclusion criteria. We will be transparent there. It's just too early to talk about it. In terms of IgG reduction required to have a clinical, meaningful effect in TED patients, you know that we typically like to triangulate by a plasma exchange or immunoadsorption data. We also believe that some of the competitive data in the FcRn class constitute an interesting data point to triangulate that.
You know that with Vyvgart we achieve a comparable IgG level reduction as with plasma exchange, and we think that will be sufficient to have a market impact in TED patients.
Operator
Your next question comes from a line of Charles Pitman from Barclays. Your line is open.
Charles Pitman
Analyst, Barclays
Hi. Thanks very much for taking my question. I've got a question on just MG, and whether or not you could give us any details on the number of new patients that were accrued in Q1 versus retreatment, whether you can give us any insight on the discontinuation rate of these patients now. Maybe just a quick follow-up, if I'm not sure you'll give us much detail on this, but on the German pricing negotiations you're about to start, how much is that likely to be? Are there any benchmarks that we should be looking at when we're considering that? Thank you.
Tim Van Hauwermeiren
CEO, argenx SE
Charles, I'll give the first question to Karl on patient numbers and what is the formal line there. Then on discontinuation, I will give the floor to Karen. Then maybe, Karl, you also have to take the question on any benchmarks for negotiated prices under the AMNOG process in Germany.
Karl Gubitz
CFO, argenx SE
Okay. Thank you, Tim. On patient numbers, Charles, thank you for the question, but we are not gonna give patient numbers now. We do say that the launch is consistent and we believe that the revenue number will be there to guide you. We're not gonna be getting into more details now. In terms of the German negotiations, we are of course at the very sensitive stage of the negotiation, so we're not gonna provide any comment. Please bear with us. We will of course start accruing for the difference between the old price and the new price effective March, i.e. you'll see an impact on total revenues in Europe, i.e. Germany, going down. We're not gonna provide any details due to the sensitivity and all. It will all be disclosed in September when the negotiations conclude.
Thank you for the question.
Karen Massey
COO, argenx SE
Thanks. Thanks, Karl, and on the discontinuation rate, I would say it's too early for us to share any numbers. The data is still maturing, but it's about what you would expect or about what we would expect at this point in launch, from what we've seen. One important factor to remember is that early on in the launch, we were getting more refractory patients. We've moved and are gaining momentum in the earlier line patients, and the discontinuation rate will reflect that, as we move forward.
Karl Gubitz
CFO, argenx SE
Thanks.
Operator
Your final question comes from the line of Simon Baker from Redburn. Your line is open.
Simon Baker
Partner and Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn
Thank you for taking my question. Another one on Vyvgart in MG. As I understand it, the only barrier to early line usage is physician awareness. I wonder if you could give us an idea of the rate at which you think physician awareness will drive earlier line usage at a greater extent, the active efforts you're doing to advance that more quickly, and the importance of the subcutaneous formulation in driving earlier line usage. Thanks so much.
Karen Massey
COO, argenx SE
Thanks for the question. It's a really good one. I would say that during, of course, the first year of launch, a lot of the momentum that we gained, as you said, was through physicians gaining awareness and early experience with Vyvgart. What we've heard, the feedback, I was at AAN last week, and I heard this consistently, is that the experience and the early experience with Vyvgart reflects what they expected from the ADAPT study. Actually what we see is the more experience as the physicians move from awareness to experience with Vyvgart, that's what's really driving the earlier line use and what's helping us with momentum in terms of moving earlier lines.
We expect that to continue, as we continue through executing on the launch, as experience grows. In terms of the subcutaneous, that will help us, as I mentioned earlier, with earlier line use. There are some patients that might not wanna move from an oral to an infusion. There are some prescribers who might prefer a subcutaneous option for logistics reasons, for patient preference, whatever it may be. We believe it opens up a whole new patient opportunity for us in the early line, to have the opportunity to have either IV or subcutaneous.
Simon Baker
Partner and Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn
Great. Thank you very much.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. We thank you for your participation today. You may now disconnect.
